paragraphs.source_en: The Round Head art is located in two kinds of landscapes. The majority of paintings are concentrated on the Tassili Plateau, representing the highest point of the study area, with the paintings being situated at an average altitude of 1500 meters above sea level. The remainder of the Round Head images are then located in lower altitudes of the Algerian Tadrart and the Acacus at an average height of 1000 meters above sea level. These two environments differ not only in terms of the altitude but also topographically.

units.source_en: The Round Head art is located in two kinds of landscapes.

The majority of paintings are concentrated on the Tassili Plateau, representing the highest point of the study area, with the paintings being situated at an average altitude of 1500 meters above sea level.

paragraphs.source_en: On the Tassili Plateau the landscape is characterised by "stone cities", i. e. agglomerations of rock shelters situated closely side by side and divided by naturally eroded corridors and by larger spaces traditionally called squares (Fig. 3-7). Stone cities may be small, containing just a few shelters, or very large with dozens of shelters. They are usually near to ancient water courses, wadies, and are often crossed by them. All painted sites on the Plateau are near to each other, so that many of them may be visited in a day's walk.

units.source_en: All painted sites on the Plateau are near to each other, so that many of them may be visited in a day's walk.

paragraphs.source_en: Regarding the Tassili Plateau, when a stone city contains paintings it is referred to as a "site" or a "painted site" regardless of the number of painted shelters, which may be sporadic or very numerous within a site. It is often impossible to distinguish the border between a painted shelter and its neighbouring one since they frequently have long walls separated by small cracks or vertical projections of the rock. Moreover, the paintings in a stone city are usually accumulated in a limited territory so that the word "site" is appropriate for a specific area of painted shelters. As for the Algerian Tadrart and the Acacus, there are no stone cities as the landscape is formed by stony hills cut by deep or moderate wadies, and this is where the shelters are located (Fig. 3-8). The word "site" is therefore used for a single shelter or at the most for a small group of shelters.
